title: In the BERJ, leading lights from the University of Manchester publish LLM slop
author: Stephen Vainker
summary: Stephen Vainker argues that the British Educational Research Association journals are publishing a steady stream of LLM-written papers and that this has now reached a paper co-authored by senior figures at the University of Manchester's Institute of Education. Using a paper on teachers' perspectives on loneliness in England and China, he points to telltale vocabulary and an everything-and-nothing tone as evidence of machine authorship. He assumes the senior co-authors played a supervisory role, but treats their names on the paper as a sign that generic LLM prose is being normalised. He adds that BERA has taken no action on fake references in multiple articles, and concludes that education research in the UK has a particular problem that further erodes its credibility with policy-makers and practitioners.
points: Vainker identifies characteristic LLM diction such as incorporate, ensure, tailored, nuanced and underscoring as markers of machine-written academic prose.
He claims BERA journals publish many LLM-generated papers and have not acted even on articles with fabricated references.
A loneliness paper co-authored by prominent Manchester academics is used to show the problem reaching leading institutions.
He argues that sophisticated-sounding language used to make a basic point costs readers effort for little gain.
He contends that complacency over slop is eroding academic education research's credibility relative to non-academic expertise.
quotes: It’s partly the everything-and-nothing tone. It solves the problem of loneliness in schools without advancing anything substantive. It’s merely a vague half-promise of a generic academic output.

By now it should be known that journals associated with the British Educational Research Association (BERA) publish an endless stream of LLM-generated papers, many of which are from China and almost all of which are from countries without robust academic integrity oversight.

I’m strongly assuming that the august co-authors had almost nothing meaningful to do with the production of the manuscript, and were acting in a merely supervisory role. However, it is in its small way an indication of generic LLM slop being normalised within BERA and within the academy more broadly.

This does make sense, and it’s a reasonable point in its way, but the relentlessly ‘sophisticated’ language to advance a very basic point means that the reader has to work quite hard for very little gain.

The point here is not that LLM writing is worthless (it is) but that if experts are prepared to put their name to such grandiose waffle, then academic expertise will soon lose much of whatever credibility it has left.
Nevertheless, it is important to continue to press the issue because education research in the UK must recognise its particular problem with LLM-writing.

Amongst policy-makers and quite probably practitioners in education, non-academic expertise has long overtaken academia in credibility. While there are various reasons for this, it is not sufficient to simply blame Michael Gove etc. and retreat into a victimised, blameless stance. BERA and education academia has become rudderless; standards have slipped.
